sentences.text: Hello, everyone.
I am Dr. Cesar Marolla, Instructor at Harvard University Division of Continuing Education.
I developed the Risk Mechanism Theory Index, RMTI, to turn what we can measure into one score that I can follow over time.
Here I apply it to liver cancer.
I start with a published case study: Lau-Min and colleagues, JAMA Network Open, 2025.
Among 4,198 patients on systemic therapy, median survival was 8.1 months, and only 20.7 percent reached second-line treatment.
I follow the tumor through four stages.
Stage one: one small tumor, inside the liver, no vessel invasion. Surgery, ablation or transplant can work.
Stage two: the tumor reaches blood vessels, or several small tumors form, still within the liver.
Stage three: larger or multiple tumors, major vein invasion, and possibly regional lymph nodes.
Stage four: cells reach distant sites, such as the lungs and bones. Treatment turns systemic.
Now I assess the data.
I use liver function, by ALBI grade, for vulnerability; concomitant liver disease for exposure; and second-line delivery, only 20.7 percent, for resilience.
This mapping is illustrative.
Then I calculate.
R equals L times E times V times one minus rho.
With these illustrative inputs, R is 0.081, band two of the fixed five-band scale.
Expected Annual Loss adds consequences.
I follow the trajectory.
At each review cycle I update vulnerability and resilience.
In this synthetic example, as delivery improves, R falls from 0.081 to 0.025, band two to band one.
It is an illustration, not a prediction.
With RMTI, I quantify risk as one score, assess it on fixed bands, and track vulnerability and resilience across cycles.
Treatment decisions stay with clinicians.
RMTI is a research prototype: uncalibrated, with synthetic examples, and not a medical device.
I am testing whether trajectory adds information beyond the current level.
Thank you for watching.
